opening.headline: ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini divide AI services out there into four types and cover how to evaluate them based on purpose and usage conditions.
body: It's not just general-purpose chat apps that will ask, 'Please verify the source of this market data and organize it.' A service that searches the web and answers with citations, a service that finds and organizes papers, a hub that collects public models, a tool that creates images, and AI that works within the browser each take on different tasks.

If you choose something based solely on its name, it may not fit its intended purpose or you may miss the terms of use. In this class, we'll take a look at provenance-based search, research services, model hubs, creation tools, and in-browser AI, and establish a baseline for what to look for in each type. At the end, we select and evaluate the services appropriate for the three tasks: research, model exploration, and draft production.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the use of source-based search, paper search, model hub, and generation tools
You can evaluate the service based on product usage conditions and limit information on the model card.
Can explain the differences between permissive licenses and conditional custom licenses, and open weight and open source.

screens.title: There are services outside of the three companies
screens.lead: Even if the request is the same, the results will vary depending on where it is made. Read the scene below and think about why service type is important.

visual.alt: Four types of service icons extending in four directions from one question in the center.
labels: Check and organize the sources of market data

paragraphs: Let's say that while writing a report, you are asked to check the source of market data and organize it. Many people just type it into their usual chat app. However, there are services that search the web in real time and add citation numbers, and there are also services that search dozens of times and organize them in the form of a report.

If you want to find papers, a service tailored to academic research is the right choice. If you want to find open models to use in your work, a hub that collects models and datasets is the right choice. If you want to create an image, you need a creation tool, and in this case, whether the created image can be used for work is determined by different terms of use for each service.
The question for this class is this. How do we classify services and by what criteria do we evaluate them? The answer lies in the things you need to check for each type.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: Are liking the results and being able to use the results in your work the same question?

screens.outro: Now that you have a sense that there are different types, let's think about our experiences so far.

screens.title: Think of external services I have used
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You will not enter or submit your answer, so think for yourself first and then click.

items.prompt: Have you ever received an answer with a link to the source?
items.answer: When there is a link, it is easy to increase faith. However, the link only provides a way to check and does not guarantee that the content is correct. In this lesson, you will see the order in which a source-based search service creates answers and see why the habit of opening citations directly is a prerequisite.

items.prompt: Have you ever spent a long time wandering around looking for papers or materials?
items.answer: The time it takes to find one can vary greatly between a general-purpose search and a purpose-built service. The research service organizes your information in the form of a report instead of repeated searches and document reading. Instead, the point is that you need to check the source of the results as well.

items.prompt: Have you ever wondered whether images created with AI can be used in your work?
items.answer: This question is not a question of technology, but of terms of use. Each creation tool has different instructions on whether commercial use is allowed, notation of beta features, and training data sources. The screens that follow provide examples of how to read these items.

screens.outro: Now that we have our experience out of the way, let's start with how origin-based search services work.

screens.title: Source-based search: Perplexity
screens.lead: Select the arrows to step through the steps to see the order in which the source-based search service answers your questions.

visual.alt: A flow chart with four steps from left to right: inquiry, search, summary, and citation.
labels: General Search / Pro Search / Research / Creating Files/Apps

steps.title: Step 1: Understand the question
steps.body: When Perplexity is asked a question, it first interprets the context and nuance of the question with a language model. Rather than simply matching keywords, we start the search by understanding what you are asking. The help explains that models such as GPT and Claude are used for this step.

steps.title: Step 2 Search the web
steps.body: Once it understands the question, it searches the Internet in real time to gather information from sources such as articles, websites, and journals. The key difference is that the general-purpose model, which answers without searching, does not know information beyond the knowledge cutoff, but this service can retrieve information beyond that date through search.

steps.title: 3 steps to summarize
steps.body: Organize the most relevant pieces of information you have gathered into one easy-to-read answer. It is a conversational summary, so it can be read quickly, but the nuance of the original text may be lost during the summarization process. That's why the next step of citation is important.

steps.title: Step 4: Indicate the source
steps.body: Each answer is accompanied by a numbered citation linking to the original text. Users can open this link to view information or read more deeply. The strength of source-based search is that you can identify supporting links, and that strength is only useful when users actually open the links.

steps.title: Search method and model selection
steps.body: Search methods are divided into general search, Pro Search, Research, and file/app creation. Pro Search searches widely across multiple sources and lets you choose an AI model to use for your answer. Research involves conducting dozens of searches and reading hundreds of sources to create a report in 2 to 4 minutes. Free users can use Pro Search a certain number of times per day, while Pro subscribers can use it more times.

screens.outro: Now that we've looked at the search type, let's move on to the research service to dig deeper.

screens.title: Research services: Deep Research and Liner
screens.lead: Select each tab to compare two research services using the same four frameworks. The final tab organizes common criteria.

tabs.label: Perplexity Deep Research
tabs.body:
**Target:** Complex topics that require in-depth research, such as finance, marketing, and technology analysis. It can be used for health, product research, and travel planning.

**How ​​it works:** Equipped with search and coding skills, it searches repeatedly, reads documents, and infers what to do next. We revise our research plan based on what we learn. The introduction explains that you search dozens of times and read hundreds of sources.

**Output:** This is a report that synthesizes the material read and can be exported as a PDF or document, or created as a Perplexity page and shared.

**Duration:** Approximately 2 to 4 minutes.

tabs.label: Liner
tabs.body:
**Targeted tasks:** Liner is divided into three branches: everyday search, academic research, and professional writing. Daily searches are handled by Liner, academic research is handled by Liner Scholar, and document creation is handled by Liner Write.

**Source:** Claims that a single citation can be viewed with just one click. It is also introduced that you can ask additional questions following the answer or solve complex topics using mind maps.

**Output:** Answer with citations, literature summary, and professional draft.

User reviews say that they use this service to check the facts of reports or verify sources before publishing, which shows what kind of work the service is aimed at.

tabs.label: common standards
tabs.body:
Putting the two services in the same framework makes comparison easier. The first is the target task: whether it is routine searching, academic research, or document writing. The second is the source indication, which is the form in which the citation is attached. Third is the form of the output: whether it is a short answer or a report. Fourth is the time it takes - how many seconds or how many minutes it takes.

The research service is also the result of a model, so you must check the source directly. Increasing repeat searches does not automatically make citations more accurate.

screens.outro: Now that we have compared research-type services, we now look at hub-type services that find the model itself.

screens.title: Public model/dataset hub and model card: Hugging Face
screens.lead: Select the number marker above the picture to see a detailed explanation. Check the sections of the hub and the items on the model card one by one.

visual.alt: A screen with three sections of the hub, Models, Datasets, and Spaces, and a model card example panel side by side.

markers.label: Composition of the hub
markers.title: Models, Datasets, Spaces
markers.body: The Hugging Face Hub document introduces that it hosts more than 2 million public models, 1.5 million datasets, and 1.5 million spaces for uploading AI apps. It is a repository that contains not only models, but also data used for learning and demo apps that can be run directly. Plans for teams or businesses to collaborate privately, as well as management features such as single sign-on and audit logs, are also included in the document.

markers.label: Model Card: Purpose
markers.title: What is this model made for?
markers.body: The model card is the model's documentation. The hub document covers model cards, evaluation results, licensing, and gated models with limited access as separate topics. The Purpose section describes what task this model is designed for. First, I check whether what I am trying to do matches the purpose written on the card. The concept of model cards was proposed by Mitchell et al. in their paper Model Cards for Model Reporting. The paper describes a model card as a short document that provides information on the context in which the model is intended to be used, the evaluation process, and performance by group.

markers.label: Model Card: Limits
markers.title: Where is it wrong or should I not use it?
markers.body: Limitations list tasks the model is not good at, known biases, or situations in which it should not be used. Just because it's public doesn't mean you can use it anywhere. If the task hits the limit, you will need to find another model or plan for additional validation.

markers.label: Model Card: License
markers.title: Can I use it commercially?
markers.body:
The license field determines under what conditions the model can be used. If you want to use it for work, first check whether it can be used commercially. Gate models with restricted access can only be downloaded if you agree to the terms of use or receive approval. The fact that a model is popular or new is no substitute for a license.

It is easier to read the license by dividing it into two parts. Permissive licenses, such as Apache 2.0, broadly permit copying, modification, and redistribution, provided that you retain a copy of the license and copyright notice and indicate that modifications were made. On the other hand, licenses customized for each model may have conditions restricting their use, so you must read the terms yourself.

Also, the fact that the weights are made available for download does not mean that they are open source. A model that only discloses the weights is called an open weight model, and the Open Source Initiative's Open Source AI Definition 1.0 requires freedom to use, study, modify, and share, as well as access to sufficient information about the training data, code used for learning and execution, and model parameters. Even if the model description says open, you must separately check whether all these conditions are met.

screens.outro: Now that we know where to look for models, let's compare the creation tools on the creation side and the browser's built-in AI.

ext.title: Mitchell et al., Model Cards for Model Reporting
Open Source Initiative, The Open Source AI Definition 1.0

screens.title: Image and video creation tools and browser built-in AI
screens.lead: Select the two states alternately to compare how the items checked vary depending on the service type.

states.label: Creation Tool: Terms of Use
states.body:
Adobe Firefly is a web app used by firefly.adobe.com. The FAQ notes that to use Firefly features, you must have an Adobe ID, follow Adobe's Generative AI usage guidelines, and be in a country where the service is available. Not available in Russia, Belarus, or China.

Regarding commercial use, it is explained that products with features not marked as beta can be used in commercial projects, and products with beta features can be used unless otherwise stated in the product.

Regarding the training data, it is informed that it was learned from licensed content such as Adobe Stock and public content whose copyright has expired, and that some exports are accompanied by Content Credentials. So when evaluating a creation tool, check its terms of use, commercial use permissions, training data policies, and display policies.

states.label: AI in Browser: Reach
states.body:
Claude in Chrome is an extension that lets you view, click, or fill out forms inside your browser. Anthropic's pilot introduction guide covers how to set up a list of sites that will be allowed by team and enterprise administrators.

These services touch my screen and login status directly. So the inspection items are closer to the scope of access than the conditions of use. Check which sites are allowed to operate, which operations are allowed for logged in work accounts, and whether administrators can restrict them to a list.

The biggest difference is that in a chat app, only the content you paste touches the model, but with browser built-in AI, it touches the entire screen that you can see. Therefore, when introducing browser built-in AI, you must first decide how much you want to entrust rather than whether the function is convenient. A key criterion in evaluating a service is whether it has a narrowing mechanism, such as an allowed site list.

screens.outro: Now that we've looked at all the service types, let's explain the flow of selection for each task as an example.

screens.title: Case Commentary 1: Research tasks and model exploration
screens.lead: The instructor explains the flow of selecting the right service for both tasks. Select the arrows to follow the journey from need to type to service to confirmation.

steps.title: Task 1: Summary of competitor trends
steps.body: The first task is to summarize competitors' recent trends and include them in a report. The report requires a link to the evidence. Because the core of the need is evidence, source-based search types come to mind first.

steps.title: Selection according to scope of investigation
steps.body: If your scope is narrow, a source-based search will suffice. If the scope is large and you need to read multiple sources repeatedly, use a research service like Deep Research. If you need academic evidence, choose a service tailored to thesis search. Either way, the final step is to try opening the citation link directly.

steps.title: Task 2: Find a public model to work with
steps.body: The second task is to find a public model to use for in-house document classification. It is a hub-type service because the demand is not the basis but the model itself. Open the candidate model's model card in Hugging Face Hub.

steps.title: Check on the model card
steps.body: Check whether the purpose of the card matches the document classification and whether there are any limitations. Lastly, check the license box to see if commercial use is allowed. I also see that if it is a gated model with limited access, you will need to agree to the terms and conditions.

steps.title: conclusion
steps.body: If the request is 'basis', it is a search or research type, and if the request is 'the model itself', it is a hub type. After choosing a service, check the confirmation items for each type. The search type includes citation links, and the hub type includes the purpose, limitations, and license of the model card. If you go down from needs to types, and from types to confirmation items, you can make judgments in the same way even when you encounter an unfamiliar service.

screens.outro: Now that we've explained the two tasks, we move on to creating a draft and evaluating the conditions of use.

screens.title: Case Commentary 2: Draft creation and use condition evaluation
screens.lead: As you select each check item, the instructor's confirmation results and reasons for judgment unfold. This is a situation where a promotional image draft is created using a creation tool.

items.prompt: Request: A promotional image draft is required. Which type of service should you choose?
items.answer: It is a type of creation tool as the need is to create images. This case evaluates Adobe Firefly as an example. The important thing is to read the terms of use first before looking at the quality of the results. Because if you like the results, your judgment becomes looser.

items.prompt: Assessment 1: Is this feature acceptable for commercial use, or is it marked as beta?
items.answer: The Firefly FAQ explains that works with features not marked as beta can be used in commercial projects, and works with beta features can also be used unless otherwise stated in the product. Therefore, make sure that the feature you want to use is marked as beta and that there are no other instructions on the screen.

items.prompt: Assessment 2: What are the sources and display policies for your training data?
items.answer: Firefly informs you that the model is trained on licensed content such as Adobe Stock and public content whose copyright has expired, and that some exports are tagged with Content Credentials. When writing promotional materials, read the sources and attribution policies to ensure they meet your organization's standards.

items.prompt: Assessment 3: Do I meet the account and region requirements?
items.answer: To use Firefly, you must have an Adobe ID, be in a country where the service is available, and follow the Generative AI usage guidelines. Violation of conditions may result in access being restricted. When writing as a team, we also make sure that all members meet this condition.

items.prompt: Conclusion: If the results are good but the conditions are not right, how do you judge it?
items.answer: If the conditions for use are not met, the decision is made not to use it, no matter how good the results are. The way to evaluate a service is to read the terms of use, training data and display policies, account and regional terms, and then look at the quality of the results. By following this order, you will avoid making the mistake of skipping conditions because you are attracted to a result you like.

screens.outro: Now that we have confirmed the evaluation criteria, we will summarize the contents of this class.

screens.title: Four types and what to check
screens.lead: Let's organize the contents of this class by grouping them into items to check by type.

paragraphs: Let's go back to the first question. How do we classify services and by what criteria do we evaluate them? The basis for distinction is demand. If the request is based on a source, then it is a source-based search; if it is a deep investigation, it is a research service; if it is a model itself, it is a model hub; if it is a product such as an image, it is a creation tool; if it is a task on the screen, it is a browser built-in AI.

The evaluation criteria comes from the fact that the check items are different for each type. The search type and research type are to directly open the citation, the hub type is to read the purpose, limitations and license of the model card, the creation tool is to check whether it is commercial use or beta, the learning data policy and account conditions, and the browser built-in AI is to check the scope of access.
I don't write any type just because the results look good. I write after first checking whether the basis is correct and the conditions of use are correct.

callout.label: standards to remember
callout.text: Before choosing a service, write down in one line what your needs are and check those types of items.

glossary.def: This is a service method that searches the web and shows links to number citations along with answers.
This service creates report-type results through repeated searches and document reading.
This is a repository of public models, datasets, and apps. Hugging Face Hub is a representative example.
This is a manual that describes the model's purpose, learning information, limitations, and license.
This is AI that looks at the screen and performs clicks or inputs within the browser. You need to check your reach.
This is a model that has been released so that the learned weights can be downloaded and used. This is not the same thing as open source AI, which requires training data information and code.

misconceptions.myth: You can trust everything as long as there is a source.
misconceptions.fact: Citations only open the way for verification. You must open the link and check for yourself whether the original text matches the answer.

misconceptions.myth: Models published on the Model Hub can be used anywhere.
misconceptions.fact: Each model has different licenses and limitations. Just because weights are published does not mean they are open source or can be used without restrictions. You should first read the model card's purpose, limitations and commercial availability of the license.

misconceptions.myth: The created images can be used commercially anywhere.
misconceptions.fact: Terms of use vary for each service. You must check the scope of commercial use, availability of beta functions, and account and regional conditions before using.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: Source-based searches answer with citations, but you open and check the citations yourself.
Research services repeatedly search multiple sources and compile them into reports.
In the public model hub, read the purpose, limitations, and license of the model card first.
The creation tool checks terms of use and commercial use, and in-browser AI checks the scope of access.
closing.reflectionLead: The following questions are for self-thinking purposes only and will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: When I receive an answer with a source attached to my work, what percentage of people actually open the link and check it, and what makes it difficult to do so?
